items.t: Essential hypertension in adults.

items.t: Reduction of cardiovascular morbidity in adults with manifest atherothrombotic cardiovascular disease (coronary heart disease, stroke or peripheral arterial disease) or type 2 diabetes with documented target organ damage.

items.t: Hypertension: usually 40 mg once daily (some respond to 20 mg); maximum 80 mg once daily. Maximum effect usually 4-8 weeks after starting.

items.t: Cardiovascular prevention: 80 mg once daily (lower doses not known to be effective). Monitor blood pressure closely when starting.

src.q: The recommended dose is 80 mg once daily.

items.t: Hyperkalaemia can be fatal in the elderly, renal insufficiency, diabetes, with other potassium-raising drugs, or intercurrent illness (dehydration, acute cardiac decompensation, acidosis). Weigh risk/benefit; monitor potassium closely in at-risk patients.

items.t: Potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g. spironolactone), potassium supplements, potassium salt substitutes: concomitant use not recommended (significant potassium rise); if used for documented hypokalaemia, use with caution and frequent potassium monitoring.

src.q: Concomitant use not recommended. Potassium sparing diuretics or potassium supplements
If concomitant use is indicated because of documented hypokalaemia, they should be used with caution and with frequent monitoring of serum potassium.

items.t: Other potassium-raising medicines (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs, heparin, ciclosporin, tacrolimus, trimethoprim): increased hyperkalaemia risk; monitor potassium closely in at-risk patients.

src.q: salt substitutes containing potassium, potassium-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers, non steroidal anti-inflammatory medicinal products (NSAIDs, including selective COX-2 inhibitors), heparin, immunosuppressives (cyclosporin or tacrolimus), and trimethoprim

items.t: NSAIDs (including COX-2 inhibitors and aspirin at anti-inflammatory doses): reduced antihypertensive effect; possible acute renal failure in compromised renal function. Use with caution, especially in the elderly; hydrate; consider monitoring renal function.

src.q: NSAIDs (i.e. acetylsalicylic acid at anti-inflammatory dosage regimens, COX-2 inhibitors and non-selective NSAIDs) may reduce the antihypertensive effect of angiotensin II receptor blockers.
Therefore, the combination should be administered with caution, especially in the elderly.

items.t: Lithium: concomitant use not recommended (raised lithium levels and toxicity); if the combination proves necessary, monitor lithium carefully. Digoxin: levels rise; monitor digoxin when starting, adjusting or stopping telmisartan.

src.q: Taking an ARB in early pregnancy is unlikely to harm your baby.
an ARB should usually be stopped as soon as you find out you are pregnant
Studies show that up to one in every three babies exposed in the womb to an ARB after 20 weeks of pregnancy develop some or all of these problems.

items.t: SPS: telmisartan can be used with caution if specifically indicated, but it is among the least preferred ARBs (long half-life, higher bioavailability) and another class is preferred. Monitor the infant for hypotension and wet nappies; neonates and infants under 2 months are at most risk.

src.q: Irbesartan and telmisartan have the longest half-lives and highest bioavailability and therefore are the least preferred options from this class.
